summary: Potassium nitrate is the active ingredient (5%) in desensitizing toothpastes used to relieve dentinal (tooth) hypersensitivity to cold, heat, sweets, acids and touch. Potassium ions diffuse along dentinal tubules and depolarize the sensory nerve, preventing repolarization and blocking pain transmission. It is used as an OTC dentifrice, brushed onto the teeth twice daily, with relief developing over about 2-4 weeks of continued use. It is for topical oral use with negligible systemic absorption; persistent sensitivity beyond 4 weeks should prompt a dental visit, and large accidental ingestion can cause nitrate toxicity (methemoglobinemia).

moa: Potassium ions from potassium nitrate diffuse along the dentinal tubules toward the pulpal nerve endings. The raised extracellular potassium concentration depolarizes the nerve and prevents it from repolarizing, blocking the synapse/nerve excitation and preventing propagation of action potentials, thereby reducing pain transmission from the sensitive tooth (a neural-depolarization mechanism rather than tubule occlusion).

pearls: Standard FDA OTC desensitizing dentifrice uses 5% potassium nitrate as the active ingredient
Works by nerve depolarization (potassium ions block pulpal nerve firing) rather than physically occluding tubules
Allow about 4 weeks of twice-daily use to judge effect; persistent sensitivity needs a dental evaluation

missed: Resume twice-daily brushing as soon as remembered; consistent continued use is needed for effect. There is no need to double up.
overdose: Ingestion of a large amount can cause nitrate/nitrite toxicity, including methemoglobinemia manifesting as cyanosis, and GI upset. Treat methemoglobinemia with methylene blue and supportive care; manage GI symptoms symptomatically.
